name: Weighted vest
lead: A weighted vest is a fitted garment that adds load to the torso, usually through removable pouches, sand bags or steel plates. For looks, it is a way to make training harder without extra equipment: it lets people keep progressing push-ups, pull-ups, dips, lunges and squats once bodyweight alone feels easy, and it raises the effort of walking, hiking and stair climbing. The chain people describe is more load per repetition or step, more muscular demand and energy expenditure, and over months a leaner, more muscular or denser-boned physique.

Loads discussed for general fitness range from roughly 5 to 20 percent of body weight, and research protocols in sprint studies have used 5 to 40 percent of body mass [1]. Vests are worn for walking and rucking-style outings, bodyweight strength work, sports conditioning and well-known challenge workouts such as the "Murph" [15]. A separate, older use is therapeutic: weighted vests, belts and blankets are used with children who have autism or ADHD on the idea that deep pressure is calming [14][16].

Most published research on weighted vests concerns older adults and bone health, sprint and jump performance in athletes, and sensory interventions in children, rather than cosmetic outcomes. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of nine randomized trials (368 participants) in middle-aged and older adults found that a vest combined with exercise improved bone mineral density and reduced body fat compared with usual activity, while adding a vest to existing exercise gave additional fat reduction but no significant added bone benefit [2]. Reviewers describe the evidence base as small and varied in protocol [2][3].

paras: Weighted vests come in fixed-weight versions, adjustable versions with removable bags or plates, and plate-carrier styles. Modern designs are described as having ergonomic shapes meant to encourage good posture, and named examples in coverage include the X-Vest and Hyper Vest PRO [14]. Fit is a practical concern: loosely fitted vests can shift, bounce and chafe during running or jumping. Wearable-resistance research distinguishes between vests, which load the trunk, and limb-worn resistance, which loads the legs or arms, and notes that they change movement mechanics differently: in a 2024 meta-analysis, limb-worn resistance reduced step frequency while vests reduced step length [4].

Weighted clothing is the broader family a vest belongs to: garments with heavy material sewn in or attached to add load to the body, usually for resistance training, leaving the hands free unlike held weights.[14] Besides torso vests the category includes neck weights, loaded backpacks, hip drags used in swimming, belts, upper-arm and wrist weights, gloves for boxing preparation, thigh weights, ankle weights and weighted footwear.[14] Backpacks are described as a way to simulate carried loads in military, firefighter and SWAT training.[14]

The mechanism offered is extra resistance from gravity, plus greater force needed to accelerate and decelerate the added mass in ballistic movements. Light weights tend to be used for long repetitive efforts and heavier garments for slow, controlled movements and bodyweight exercises.[14] The article also reports a study in which vest walking raised metabolic cost, relative exercise intensity and skeletal loading.[14]

Loaded carrying has a long military pedigree. Wikipedia's article on loaded marching, which covers rucking, notes that Roman recruits trained with loads of about 20 kg over long distances, and that modern armies test loaded marches annually [17]. Civilian "rucking" with a weighted pack is the walking-oriented cousin of vest wear.

People who train for appearance use a vest to keep bodyweight exercises such as push-ups, pull-ups and dips progressing once bodyweight alone becomes easy, and to make walking, hiking or stair work a heavier session. Because the load rides on the torso, the hands stay free and the movement pattern stays close to the unloaded version, which is one reason home-gym lifters adopt it [14].

Users on T Nation, a bodybuilding forum, discuss vests in threads about home gyms and tactical training, and challenge workouts built around a fixed vest load circulate there [18]. Typical talking points are choosing a vest weight that fits the equipment on hand, doubling repetitions when the vest is light, and keeping sessions short and high in volume [18].

The best-known vest workout is the Murph. Navy lieutenant Michael P. Murphy created a routine he called "Body Armor" and did it in a 16.4 lb (7.4 kg) vest carried on deployment; it combines two one-mile runs with 100 pull-ups, 200 push-ups and 300 air squats [15]. Murphy died on June 28, 2005 in Afghanistan, and CrossFit founder Greg Glassman posted the workout as the Workout of the Day on August 17, 2005 [15]. It is now commonly done on Memorial Day at gyms, bases and ships and by civilians [15].
Strength coach Jim Wendler's "Walrus" challenge is another vest-based session built around chin-ups, push-ups or dips and lunges, and forum posters describe scaling it to 25 to 45 lb vests [18].

Weighted vests, belts and blankets are also used in sensory integration therapy for children with autism and other developmental conditions, on the idea that deep pressure gives calming proprioceptive feedback.[14][16] The practice began in the United States as autism therapy, and by 2017 vests were being worn voluntarily in some public schools in Hamburg, Germany, for up to 30 minutes at a time, which drew media attention and criticism because long-term studies are lacking [16]. Wikipedia notes that research in this setting has not shown significant improvement, a 2015 review of autism treatments found one small positive study and six with no benefit, and a systematic review of sensory interventions in school settings reported that the efficacy of vests varies with the protocol of use [3][14][16][19]. This is a separate use from fitness loading.

Added load raises the mechanical work of each step or repetition, which increases muscular demand and energy expenditure. In bone research, the rationale is that skeletal tissue responds to mechanical loading, so externally replacing weight lost during dieting may limit bone loss [5]. In sprint research, vests reduce velocity and power acutely and increase ground contact time, which is the basis for their use as resisted-sprint training [1][4]. Wake Forest researchers who re-analysed trial data reported that vest wearers who spent more time upright and stepping showed better bone outcomes, and suggested standing and moving increase the load the vest delivers [6].

In older adults, a 2026 narrative review of 15 articles reported that benefits tended to appear with task-based, progressively loaded protocols, including improvements in some neuromuscular measures and, in some settings, maintenance of hip bone density, whereas low-load wear-only protocols generally did not show measurable musculoskeletal improvements [3]. The Wake Forest release quoted lead author Jason Fanning saying that people given vests need training to be up and moving [6].

For sprinting, an 11-study systematic review found that vest loads between 5 and 40 percent of body mass slowed 10 to 50 m sprint times by 4.1 to 16.9 percent acutely and lengthened ground contact, while longitudinal studies of 3 to 7 weeks at 5.6 to 18.9 percent of body mass reported small improvements in velocity and times [1]. A 2024 meta-analysis of 25 studies found no chronic difference in sprint time for vests, although few trials existed [4]. In a 7-week trial of 20 lacrosse players, sled and vest groups did not differ significantly from an unresisted group [11].

For jumping, a randomized crossover in 18 high school female athletes found that a dynamic warm-up with a vest at 2 percent of body mass was associated with longer standing long jumps than static stretching [12].

Studies that measure body composition come mainly from middle-aged and older adults and from small circuit-training trials. The meta-analysis reported additional fat reduction when a vest was added to exercise (0.73 kg versus exercise alone) and a 2.67 kg lower fat mass than usual activity [2]. An 8-week trial in 36 normal-weight obese women reported that vest circuit training was associated with greater skeletal muscle mass gain and lower resistin and insulin resistance than bodyweight circuits [13].

Reviews in older adults advise screening, conservative starting loads, gradual progression and monitoring; adverse events in those trials were mostly mild, though one trial recorded more falls [3]. Heavier loads can increase stress on knees, hips and the lower back, according to general exercise guidance, and a vest can slow walking or running pace. Wikipedia's overview of weighted clothing adds that vests can shear or shift during pull-ups or high-range push-ups, especially with shoulder tightness, and that heavy nylon or neoprene vests can restrict breathing and cause overheating.[14] One biomechanical study in children and adolescents with autism found that vest loads did not alter spatial-temporal gait parameters [7].

A 12-month randomized trial (INVEST in Bone Health) assigned 150 older adults with obesity to diet-induced weight loss alone, weight loss plus a vest worn about 8 hours a day (titrated to replace up to 10 percent of lost weight) or weight loss plus supervised resistance training [5]. Weight loss was 9.0 to 11.2 percent in all groups, hip bone density fell by 1.2 to 1.9 percent in all groups, and the vest group did not differ significantly from weight loss alone; the vest was consistent with noninferiority to resistance training [5].

A 2026 meta-analysis pooled nine trials of vests in middle-aged and older adults: femoral neck and lumbar spine density were higher with vest plus exercise than usual activity, and body fat lower [2]. Earlier work includes a nine-month study of 44 postmenopausal women in which vest-based lower-body exercise improved stability, raised lower-body strength 16 to 33 percent and leg lean mass 3.5 percent without a bone change [9]; a five-year study of 18 women in which vest plus jumping was associated with hip bone density maintenance [8]; and a 12-week pilot of 21 older women in which vest-based high-velocity training improved leg power [10]. Athletic studies include sled-versus-vest sprint training [11], vest warm-ups [12] and sprint reviews [1][4]. Studies of weighted vests in children with sensory conditions are reviewed separately [3][16].

In physique-focused communities, vests are discussed as a way to add load to bodyweight movements and walking, and as a means of increasing calorie burn on low-intensity cardio. Challenge workouts such as the Murph and the Walrus are shared as vest sessions [15][18]. Home-gym threads treat the vest as an inexpensive piece of equipment for adding resistance to pull-up and dip training [18].

lore.intro: Vests come up in home-gym, tactical-fitness and strength-challenge threads, where posters trade vest weights and workout formats [18]. Research descriptions below are drawn from published trials and reviews.

claims.claim: A vest makes bodyweight exercises progressive.
claims.believers: Posters describe adding a vest to pull-ups, dips, push-ups and lunges when bodyweight is no longer challenging, and scaling challenge workouts to whatever vest weight they own [18].
claims.experts: Studies of vests in exercise have mostly used older adults or athletes; a trial in normal-weight obese women reported greater skeletal muscle mass gain with vest circuits than bodyweight circuits [13].

claims.claim: Wearing a vest while walking builds bone.
claims.believers: Proponents cite the idea that bone responds to load and that vests replace weight lost in dieting [5].
claims.experts: A 12-month trial found hip bone loss in all arms, with no significant difference from weight loss alone [5]; a meta-analysis found higher bone density with vest plus exercise versus usual activity [2]; a Wake Forest analysis linked benefit to time upright and stepping [6].

claims.claim: A vest adds fat loss on top of exercise.
claims.believers: Users say the extra load raises the calorie cost of walking and cardio.
claims.experts: A 2026 meta-analysis reported 0.73 kg additional fat reduction versus exercise alone, and one study reported greater energy cost of vest walking [2][14].

claims.claim: Vest sprint training makes you faster.
claims.believers: Resisted-sprint practitioners use vests on the idea that overload builds force.
claims.experts: Reviews report acute slowing and small longitudinal gains, and a 2024 meta-analysis found no chronic difference for vests; a lacrosse trial found no advantage over unresisted sprinting [1][4][11].

claims.claim: A light vest in the warm-up improves jumping.
claims.believers: Athletes use light vests in dynamic warm-ups.
claims.experts: One randomized crossover in 18 female athletes found longer long jumps after a warm-up with a 2 percent vest than after static stretching [12].

claims.claim: Weighted vests calm children with autism or ADHD.
claims.believers: Parents and some schools use vests on the idea that deep pressure is soothing [16].
claims.experts: Reviews report no significant improvement in several trials, and a systematic review found efficacy varied with protocol [3][14][16].

claims.claim: Heavy vests strain the joints and shoulders.
claims.believers: Some lifters recommend starting light and progressing gradually.
claims.experts: Guidance in older-adult reviews advises conservative starts and monitoring [3]; Wikipedia notes vest shearing and heat concerns [14].

angle.text: People wear a vest to progress bodyweight exercises and to make walking or hiking a heavier session. Studies in older adults and in women doing circuit training have measured changes in body fat, lean mass and bone density with vest training [2][13].
